cultivar: Chinary bushes (Camellia sinensis var. sinensis) descended from nineteenth-century Chinese seed, plus a few local clones
processing: Fully oxidised orthodox black tea made in small factories with a wither, light rolling, oxidation and firing; the leaf is kept largely whole and the style sits between a Darjeeling and a gentle Assam.
harvest_season: April to October; the first flush in April–May is the best of the year.
appearance_dry: Twisted brown-olive leaf with some lighter tips.
taste_profile: Light-bodied with a nutty, honeyed sweetness and a faint floral, Darjeeling-like lift; low in tannin.

brewing.notes: Just under the boil, three to four minutes, no milk; too delicate to carry it.

vintage_note: Sold by garden and flush with the year, mostly within India through the Palampur cooperative factory and a few private estates (Wah Tea Estate, Dharmsala Tea Company), and abroad as occasional single lots from speciality importers. Kangra tea holds a geographical indication. Spring lots are on sale from May; drink within a year or two.
description:
Kangra tea comes from the Kangra valley in Himachal Pradesh, on the southern flank of the Dhauladhar range around Palampur and Dharamsala, one of the oldest and smallest tea districts in India. Bushes planted from Chinese seed in the mid-nineteenth century still carry much of the crop, and the valley makes both black and green tea in a light, delicate style that sits between Darjeeling and a gentle Assam.

The black tea is fully oxidised orthodox manufacture in small factories: a wither, light rolling, oxidation and firing, with the leaf kept largely whole. Kangra's altitude is modest, around 900 to 1,400 metres, but its cool springs and Chinary bushes give the leaf a Darjeeling-like fragrance without Darjeeling's sharp edge.

The cup is bright amber and light-bodied, with a nutty, honeyed sweetness, a faint floral lift and low tannin. Brew it with water around 90 °C for three to four minutes and drink it plain; it is too delicate to carry milk. The first flush in April and May is the best of the year.

It is sold by garden and flush, with the year, and the name is protected as a geographical indication. Production is tiny and most of it stays in India, sold through the Palampur cooperative factory and a few private estates (Wah Tea Estate and the Dharmsala Tea Company are the names you will see), so abroad it appears as single lots from speciality importers. Drink it within a year or two.

If you are passing through, Palampur's gardens and factory shops are the easiest place to taste a range of lots side by side.
